page.label: guardEffectivenessDesc
page.text: The town watch maintains standard patrol coverage. Effective against opportunistic crime; less effective against organized operations that can plan around patrol routes. A functioning court and prison mean crimes carry real consequences. Walls control entry points and give the guard a chokehold on smuggling routes.
Spitzplatz is at the point where the arrangements are sufficient and nothing is spare. One more demand on them and the town would be choosing which pressure to leave uncovered.

page.label: safetyLabel
page.text: Moderate

page.label: safetyDesc
page.text: A mix of safer and more exposed areas. The watch covers the main paths; quieter spots after dark carry genuine risk. Residents know which corners to avoid. The walls contain the problem somewhat: crime is concentrated inside rather than spilling into the surrounding territory.
The balance at Spitzplatz sits where either side could take it. A thinner watch or a bolder operator would show up in the returns within the season, and nothing else would need to change.

page.label: criminalStructure
page.text: Organized Syndicate

page.label: criminalStructure.note
page.text: A structured criminal hierarchy controls what crime is permitted. Predictable rules, a hierarchy to negotiate with. Or cross. Random violence is suppressed because it draws enforcement. The real danger is systematic: protection, extortion, corruption of officials.
There is very little street violence at Spitzplatz and it is not the watch's doing. A structured interest suppresses what draws enforcement, and does it more thoroughly than the watch could.
Whatever is being run at Spitzplatz is being run outside the hall, and the town's dealings with the hall are the town's dealings with the hall.
Spitzplatz controls its own entry points. That is what a perimeter buys: not invulnerability, but the choice of where anything happens.
There are people walking the town at Spitzplatz at night, and the town's sense of itself rests more on that than on anything at the gate.
A stranger at Spitzplatz finds a hall whose business is the sort of trouble a garrison is the wrong instrument for, and finds it busy.
Spitzplatz keeps arcane provision in its defenses: detection, wards, and an answer to things that conventional arrangements cannot see coming.

faces: A clerk in the hall says a man waits because the matter before his is being heard properly.
A drover says a man waits because nobody has said whose business he is.
A traveller's complaint is heard like any other, by a magistrate's account. Whether the traveller stays for it is the traveller's own affair.
At the tavern they say a man is called in for who he knows and let out for what he can pay.
The wage is the same whether the night is quiet or a man is walked in, one of the watch says.
A soldier reckons a stranger stopped at the gate is the garrison's until his business is asked. After that he is the watch's.
A guild member says the trades pay for the waiting twice, in the man who waits and in the work that waits with him.
The stallholders say a stranger cheated at the market is told where to bring it. A stallholder cheated by a stranger is told the same, after the stranger has gone.
Those who keep the gate say a stranger with a complaint against him waits at the gate until somebody comes for him.
unit.rendered: At the tavern they say a man is called in for who he knows and let out for what he can pay.
unit.spine: A traveller who brings a complaint here is shown where it is heard and where the person he names would be kept.

roster.role: a master of one of the crafts

faces: The watch says the purse that pays it is opened last.
The soldiers say they are paid out of the same purse and in the same order.
The hall's answer, when the wage is raised, is the grain store.
The guilds say the trades made the provision and the hall made the shortfall.
A stranger smells grain at the store door and hears the wage complained of at the tavern.
A local priest reports that the parish asks for nothing the town has not already promised it, and does not say what it has been given.
Asked about the purse, the hall talks about the grain store, and asked again, talks about the grain store again.
The court says nobody has brought it the question of the watch's wage. It does not expect the hall to.

faces: A local priest says a stranger asks for a house and is given a person, and nobody born here asks for the house.
Grain is hard to keep here, those who sell at the market say, for anybody without a door of their own in the town.
At the tavern they say strangers walk up to look at the store, and nobody here does.
Strangers ask the watch where the grain is kept, the watch says, and nobody has ever asked it where the sick are.
A guild member reckons what a stranger takes for provision is a store the trades filled and cannot open.
Those who hear disputes say a stranger's questions about the store are ordinary and the ones about the sick are new to them.
